recentItems.title: AI rivals join forces calling for slowdown in technology development | Indonesian ship rescue
recentItems.description:
Some of the biggest names in tech have come out in support of slowing down the development of artificial intelligence, fearing it could soon get out of control.

The CEO of Anthropic, supported by Elon Musk and OpenAI's Sam Altman, are calling for AI companies to allow more time to manage the risks, which include autonomous cyberattacks and the development of biological weapons.

The move was sparked by an Anthropic employee, who resigned over fears that AI expansion would lead to human extinction in the immediate future.

recentItems.title: Anthony Albanese defends late mother after Pauline Hanson's criticism
recentItems.description:
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has criticised Pauline Hanson over comments about his late mother living in public housing for decades, saying he was proud of his upbringing and defending his mother as "way out of Pauline Hanson's league". 

"She made comments about me being complaining about being growing up in public housing — nothing could be further from the truth," Albanese told reporters in Sydney on Sunday.

The comments follow resurfaced footage from Hanson's February appearance on a podcast, in which she mimicked Albanese crying while mocking his account of growing up in social housing in Sydney's inner west.

She argued Albanese's mother should not have remained in the same public housing property all her life.

On Friday, Hanson doubled down on those comments, saying the prime minister "complains about his housing commission upbringing".

Read more: https://www.sbs.com.au/news/article/proud-to-be-a-houso-albo-responds-hansons-comments-on-late-mother/xl6ak28b9

recentItems.title: The new world map explained
recentItems.description:
The UN's new world map of continental landmasses, has caused a bit of controversy. 

The new map — known as the Equal Earth cartographic projection — was voted on at the UN General Assembly and spearheaded by several African countries to ensure a "more accurate representation" of landmasses. 

Read more: https://bit.ly/46IHyUg

recentItems.title: Israeli settlements in occupied West Bank explained
recentItems.description:
Britain, France and Canada among a dozen countries who have announced plans to block imports from Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.

Israel responded swiftly by saying it will close Britain's consulate in East Jerusalem within 30 days and impose travel bans on some British officials.

Israel has established more than 580 settlements and outposts in the West Bank, fragmenting Palestinian territory. Experts say Israel's latest settlement plants would make a two-state solution virtually impossible.

recentItems.title: Houthis seize Red Sea territory | Oil supply crisis deepens as Saudi Arabia pipeline struck
recentItems.description:
audi Arabia has shut down a key pipeline it's been using to bypass the Strait of Hormuz … putting further pressure on global oil supplies.

The Saudi energy ministry said it had temporarily shut the pipeline as a precaution after it came under aerial attack.

At the same time, Yemen's Houthis have tightened their grip on the Red Sea, seizing more territory including a strategic island in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.

recentItems.title: Anton Enus signs off after 27 years with SBS News
recentItems.description:
When you next sit down to watch SBS World News on a Friday or Saturday night, you’ll no doubt be missing a familiar face.

After 27 years of delivering the world’s biggest stories, our beloved presenter Anton Enus has signed off for the last time – closing a huge chapter in an extraordinary career.

Anton’s calm voice has been there to guide us through some of the most important issues of the 21st Century.

Here’s a brief look back on his incredible contribution to SBS News over the years.

Anton, we hope you enjoy watching from afar.

To revisit Anton’s last SBS World News bulletin, head to: https://youtu.be/Qd3CAXcXYtE

recentItems.title: Could Germany’s firewall to keep the far-right out come crashing down?
recentItems.description:
Germany’s AfD party caused a political earthquake this week after it collected 44 per cent of the vote in an election in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt.

The party is set to be just three seats short of a majority government, marking the first time a German far-right party has been this close to power since the end of World War II.

The results were far worse than German chancellor Friedrich Merz expected, who’s own Christian Democratic Union party saw their vote share halved.

Despite a steady rise in popularity over the more than a decade, the AfD has been kept at arm’s length by a so-called “firewall”, meaning most parties have ruled out formally cooperating with them.

But could this result cause the firewall to come crashing down – and could the AfD finally find another party willing to help it form a government?

For more on this story, watch the World News Weekly podcast @sbsnews_au (link in bio)
